title: Government to fold family planning field staff into a new primary healthcare department
excerpt: A Department of Primary Healthcare would bring three groups of field workers under one roof. A committee has 20 working days to design it.
content:
The government will create a Department of Primary Healthcare by restructuring the Directorate General of Family Planning (DGFP), The Daily Star reported on 9 November. The decision was taken at a health ministry meeting on 6 October.

What would change

The new department would bring together three groups of field workers who now run separate programmes:

  • health assistants under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS);
  • community health care providers at community clinics, under the Community Clinic Health Assistance Trust;
  • family welfare assistants and family planning inspectors under the DGFP.

They would work from planned health and wellbeing centres at union level in rural areas and ward level in city corporations, and visit every household at least once every two months for basic checks, while continuing vaccination and contraceptive distribution.

The bigger plan

The move is part of a wider overhaul the government announced on 6 November. It plans Tk 119.93 billion for 14,634 primary healthcare hubs and 1,631 centres between December 2026 and December 2029, and 100,000 new health workers over three years on top of about 40,000 existing ones. Recruitment of the first 30,000 has begun, according to BSS. All 503 upazila health complexes are to become 151-bed hospitals.

A seven-member committee led by an additional secretary of the Health Services Division will design the department’s structure, staffing and career plans, and has 20 working days to report.

Who said what

SM Ziauddin Hyder, the prime minister’s special assistant on health, proposed the restructuring, according to meeting minutes. ANM Bazlur Rashid, secretary of the Health Services Division, said the government wants to keep family planning a priority while integrating it. “The initiative is at a very preliminary stage,” he said.

Professor Be-Nazir Ahmed, former director of disease control at DGHS, urged more discussion: “Once a separate structure is set up, it may be difficult to reverse it later.”

Why it matters

Bangladesh’s family planning programme, built on door-to-door field workers, is one of its best-known development successes. Merging those workers into a general primary healthcare service could improve coverage, or could dilute family planning at a time when The Daily Star has reported contraceptive shortages and the fertility rate has risen. NGOs running maternal health, family planning and community clinic programmes will need to plan around new structures and reporting lines.

What to watch

The committee’s report, whether family planning keeps a dedicated budget line, and how NGO-run satellite clinics and community health workers fit into the new department.
